title: Check yourself: what counts as a functional interface, and what the int versions buy

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An interface declares two abstract methods: `boolean test(String s)` and `boolean equals(Object o)`. Per this page, can a lambda implement it?

options.text: No: with two abstract methods there is no single method to target
options.says: The page says methods inherited from Object do not count toward the abstract method count, so only test is counted.

options.text: Yes: a method every class inherits is left out of that count
options.says: The page's key points say methods inherited from Object don't count, which leaves test as the one abstract method.

options.text: Only after the second method is given a default body there
options.says: The page needs no default body here: a method inherited from Object is simply not counted.

questions.stem: In this page's guidelines for choosing an interface, what are primitive specializations such as `IntPredicate` for?

options.text: Lazy initialization, and factory methods that generate values on demand
options.says: The page's guidelines list lazy initialization and factory methods under Supplier<T>, not under the primitive specializations.

options.text: Side effects, such as logging, monitoring and database updates
options.says: The page's guidelines list side effects such as logging and database updates under Consumer<T>, not under the primitive specializations.

options.text: Performance, by avoiding the boxing and unboxing overhead of wrappers
options.says: The page's guidelines say to use primitive specializations for performance with primitives, avoiding boxing/unboxing overhead.

concepts: The primitive specializations exist to avoid the cost of boxing and unboxing.
Abstract methods that restate a public method of Object do not count toward the single abstract method.
